raw_source: STATEMENT: Shor's algorithm factors integers and computes discrete logarithms in polynomial time on an ideal quantum computer; no polynomial-time classical factoring algorithm is known.

raw_source: STATEMENT: Grover's algorithm finds a marked item among N in about √N queries, and this is optimal for unstructured search.
VERIFICATION: Published results (Grover 1996; Bennett et al. 1997).
ground_truth.statement: Grover's algorithm finds a marked item among N in about √N queries, and this is optimal for unstructured search.

raw_source: EXPECTED OUTPUT: Grover ≈ (π/4)·√N ≈ 785 iterations; classical expected ≈ 500,000 checks
VERIFICATION: Hand calculation (E01); confirm with a calculator.

raw_source: STATEMENT: Under idealised Grover analysis, a k-bit symmetric key has effective quantum search cost ≈ 2^(k/2) (AES-128 → 2⁶⁴; AES-256 → 2¹²⁸).
VERIFICATION: Arithmetic; "idealised" means ignoring error-correction overhead and parallelisation limits.
ground_truth.statement: Under idealised Grover analysis, a k-bit symmetric key has effective quantum search cost ≈ 2^(k/2) (AES-128 → 2⁶⁴; AES-256 → 2¹²⁸).

raw_source: STATEMENT: Public-key schemes based on integer factoring or discrete logarithms (RSA, Diffie–Hellman, elliptic-curve cryptography) are vulnerable to Shor-type algorithms; symmetric ciphers and hash functions are affected only by Grover-type quadratic speedups.

raw_source: STATEMENT: Gidney (Google Quantum AI, 2025) estimated that a 2048-bit RSA integer could be factored in under a week by a quantum computer with fewer than one million noisy qubits, assuming a square grid with nearest-neighbour connections, 0.1% uniform gate error, 1 µs surface-code cycle and 10 µs control reaction time; the 2019 Gidney–Ekerå estimate was about 20 million qubits and 8 hours.
